newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch electricity branches out into wood trimmings.
newsitem.headline: Dutch electricity branches out into wood trimmings.

text.p: The Dutch electricity sector, keen to branch away from fossil fuels, will next year begin the construction of three power stations fired with waste wood, the companies said on Tuesday.

The Provinciaal Noordbrabantse Energie Maatschappij (PNEM), an energy supply company in the southern Dutch province of North Brabant, will be the first when it begins construction of two 10 megawatt (MW) power stations from the start of 1997.
The two stations combined will be capable of supply 50,000 domestic customers when they start up in late 1998 or early 1999.
"It is a first (in the Netherlands)," said PNEM spokesman, Rudolf Kool.
The construction follows a deal PNEM clinched with the Dutch state forestry agency to supply the company with wood trimmings and other wood waste.
"It will only be the spare wood from maintaining the forests," said Kool.

The second plant, a 30 MW station which will devour spare wood and other biomass, will be built in the province of Noord Holland, in the west of the country. The project will team up the province and the regional electricity supply company, Energie Noord West (ENW).

"We're in the process of preparing a plant. We have the financing and, hopefully, it will ready at the end of 1998...There are already several (companies) who want to buy the electricity," said Gert de Boer, the chairman of the steering committee.
PNEM already has a scheme allowing customers to purchase so-called "green power" at a slightly higher rate than normal.

PNEM charges normal electricity users at a rate of 19 guilder cents per kilowatt-hour (kwh), a rate that rises to 22.5 cents after tax. The green power comes at a cost of 27.61 cents, inclusive of a lower rate of tax.

Kool says demand for renewable fuel is likely to increase if the European Union agrees that countries may apply a lower rate of VAT on electricity from renewable sources. The Dutch finance ministry confirmed the government's interest in the matter and suggested the Netherlands would use its presidency of the EU from January to press for policy agreement.
"We are waiting for a proposal from their (the EU's) side...and we plan to encourage the Commission to form a proposal on that matter," a finance ministry spokesman said.

According to Kool, the proposal the EU are considering would narrow the gap between green and fossil fuel electricity by three to four cents. He also hopes economies of scale will aid energy production from renewable sources.
"By increasing the efficiency of renewable power stations, we will also reduce the cost of green power," Kool said.
Even so, the construction of the wood-fired power stations is a sign that demand has outstripped supply.
"There is not enough wind power in our province to meet market demand," Kool said.
PNEM currently supplies 7,000 consumers with electricity principally derived from wind power.

In due course, Dutch energy suppliers will also be obliged at least some electricity derived from renewable sources. Renewables currently make up about one percent of Dutch energy consumption, but the government is hoping that share will rise to 10 percent by 2020.
PNEM believes such a target is within reach once they have also constructed two 4 MW hydro-electricity plants on the river Maas and a few more wind stations.
"We like to think we can meet the (10 percent) target," said Kool.
-- Philip Blenkinsop, Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5004
